extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, marketers, publishers, ad agencies, platform operators, and digital media professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and presenting native advertising so consumers can identify it as advertising and not be deceived; covers when disclosures are required and how to make them clear, prominent, and effective across digital contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency ('watchword is transparency')
rubrics_metrics.description: "From the FTC’s perspective, the watchword is transparency. An advertisement or promotional message shouldn’t suggest or imply to consumers that it’s anything other than an ad."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If content suggests it is independent or editorial when it is sponsored, that format is deceptive. Some native ads may be obviously commercial and not need disclosure; others require a disclosure that is clear and prominent. This is the overarching principle that governs all other guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive act/practice and materiality standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the FTC Act, an act or practice is deceptive if there is a material misrepresentation or omission of information that is likely to mislead the consumer acting reasonably in the circumstances. A misrepresentation is material if it is likely to affect consumers’ choices or conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess deception by the likely effect on reasonable consumers. Materiality focuses on whether knowing the truth about the content’s commercial nature would affect consumer decisions. Use this to determine whether a disclosure is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net impression / consider overall context and format
rubrics_metrics.description: "In evaluating whether an ad is deceptive, the FTC considers the net impression the ad conveys to consumers. ... both what the ad says and the format it uses to convey that information will be relevant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate isolated phrases or visuals in a vacuum. Consider text, images, sounds, placement, and overall site/feed context. Clarifying information must be clear and prominent to overcome a misleading net impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading about source or independence is deceptive
rubrics_metrics.description: It is deceptive to mislead consumers about the commercial nature of content or to convey expressly or by implication that content is independent, impartial, or from a source other than the sponsoring advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the source is material because it affects interaction and credibility. Ads that mimic editorial content or news format risk conveying false independence and require corrective disclosure or different formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format-based deception can exist even if product claims are truthful
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC considers misleadingly formatted ads to be deceptive regardless of whether the underlying product claims that are conveyed to consumers are truthful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with accurate product claims, disguising advertising as editorial or independent content violates truth-in-advertising principles; remedy by clear labeling and/or format differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that native ads be identifiable before click (no deceptive door openers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers are responsible for ensuring that native ads are identifiable as advertising before consumers arrive at the main advertising page. The FTC prohibits use of "deceptive door openers" to induce consumers to view advertising content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures or other cues must appear in feeds, headlines, thumbnails, or wherever consumers first encounter the content (not only on the click-through page). Commission has held that deception at first contact can violate the law even if corrected later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess recognizability on the publisher main page as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: "In assessing whether a native ad presented on the main page of a publisher site is recognizable as advertising to consumers, advertisers should consider the ad as a whole... Factors to weigh include an ad’s overall appearance; the similarity of its written, spoken, or visual style or subject matter to non-advertising content ... and the degree to which it is distinguishable from other content on the publisher site."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare topic, tone, visuals, fonts, layout, and placement to the site’s editorial content. Examples show that when subject matter differs and wording signals commerce, disclosure might be unnecessary; when style and topic match editorial content, disclosure will likely be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for disclosures both on publisher main page and click-through pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Because consumers can navigate to the advertising without first going to the publisher site, a disclosure just on the publisher’s site may not be sufficient. Disclosures are needed both on the publisher’s site and the click- or tap-into page on which the complete ad appears, unless the click-into page is obviously an ad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place disclosures at each point consumers may encounter the content (feed, widget, social post, search result, click-through landing page) unless the landing page itself makes commercial nature obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity to surrounding content increases disclosure necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more a native ad is similar in format and topic to content on the publisher’s site, the more likely that a disclosure will be necessary to prevent deception."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an ad mirrors editorial look, tone, subject matter, images, or layout, stronger and more prominent disclosures are required. Use the examples to evaluate gradations of similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain disclosures when content is republished or shared
rubrics_metrics.description: "Disclosures should remain when native ads are republished by others in non-paid search results, social media, email, or other media."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sharable links, snippets, and social tags preserve disclosures (e.g., include disclosure at beginning of title tag or at start of URL snippet). Plan for third-party republication scenarios so disclosures travel with content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single disclosure insufficient for mixed groupings; label individual items
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a grouping of content items contains a mix of advertising and non-advertising content, a single disclosure should not be used because consumers are not likely to know to which content items the disclosure relates. Native ads should be individually labeled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For content recommendation widgets or grouped feeds, individually mark each sponsored item or use clear visual cues (distinct borders, shading) plus per-item disclosure so consumers know which items are ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity and placement: place disclosures near focal points
rubrics_metrics.description: "Place disclosures on the main page of a publisher site where consumers will notice them and easily identify the content to which the disclosure applies... Place disclosures in front of or above the headline of the native ad."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures should be placed at or immediately adjacent to the ad’s focal point (headline, thumbnail). Avoid placing disclosures to the right or below in left-to-right reading contexts or in locations consumers are unlikely to see before clicking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place disclosures on focal image/thumbnail when image is focal point
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a native ad’s focal point is an image or graphic, a disclosure might need to appear directly on the focal point itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When thumbnails or images draw attention more than text (e.g., video thumbnails), overlay a readable disclosure on the image so it cannot be overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures should remain visible on click-into page near where users look first
rubrics_metrics.description: "Once consumers arrive on the click- or tap-into page where the complete native ad appears, disclosures should be placed as close as possible to where they will look first... For articles, disclosures therefore should be placed as close as possible to the headline."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burying disclosures far above or to the right of the headline; put them where readers’ eyes go first so they see the commercial attribution before consuming the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for multimedia disclosures: before the advertising message
rubrics_metrics.description: "In multimedia ads, a disclosure should be delivered to consumers before they receive the advertising message to which it relates. Delivering disclosures during or after an advertising message increases the risk consumers will miss the necessary disclosure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present visual disclosures on-screen long enough to read and comprehend; for audio, speak at an understandable cadence and volume. But avoid placing disclosures so early in long programming that consumers fail to link them to the later ad content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence: size, color, contrast, duration, and borders
rubrics_metrics.description: "Advertising disclosures should stand out so consumers can easily read or hear them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large readable fonts appropriate to device screens, strong color contrast with backgrounds, saturated shading, and prominent borders. For multimedia, display visual disclosures long enough to be read; audio disclosures should be loud enough and spoken clearly. Visual cues in addition to color (borders, outlines) help users who cannot perceive color differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of meaning / plain language required
rubrics_metrics.description: "Disclosures must be understandable... Disclosures should be in plain language that is as straightforward as possible... Advertisers should avoid using technical or industry jargon; unfamiliar icons or abbreviations; company logos or brand names unaccompanied by a clear text disclosure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms likely to be understood such as “Ad,” “Advertisement,” “Paid Advertisement,” or “Sponsored Advertising Content.” Avoid ambiguous terms like “Promoted” or “Promoted Stories” and inconsistent or varying terminology on the same site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent terminology across a publisher site
rubrics_metrics.description: "Using consistent terminology to identify ads on the same publisher site decreases the likelihood that consumers will misunderstand a native ad’s disclosure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain one clear label for sponsored content across the site (do not use different words in different places to mean the same thing, or the same term to mean different things).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess disclosures from the perspective of the reasonable consumer (including targeted audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Disclosures must be clear and prominent on all devices and platforms... In assessing effectiveness, disclosures should be considered from the perspective of a reasonable consumer. When ads are targeted to a specific audience, the relevant perspective is that of a reasonable or ordinary member of the targeted group."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test disclosures with the intended audience; if a significant minority of reasonable consumers do not notice, process, or comprehend the disclosure, improve its clarity/prominence. Consider device formats and user behavior patterns for that audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio disclosure specifics (volume, cadence, plain words)
rubrics_metrics.description: For audio disclosures: "read at a cadence that’s easy for consumers to follow and in words consumers will understand" and be at sufficient volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make audio disclosures clear, spoken at comfortable speed, and loud enough to be heard over other audio. Combine with on-screen visual disclosure in multimedia when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Icons, logos, and abbreviations alone are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Unfamiliar icons or abbreviations; Company logos or brand names unaccompanied by a clear text disclosure" should be avoided as primary disclosures because they are not likely adequate to signal that content is commercial advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using an icon or logo, pair it with explicit plain-language text (e.g., 'Ad' or 'Sponsored') so consumers recognize the commercial nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility extends beyond advertisers to all participants
rubrics_metrics.description: "The FTC’s Enforcement Policy Statement ... doesn’t apply just to advertisers. ... In appropriate circumstances, the FTC has taken action against other parties who helped create deceptive advertising content – for example, ad agencies and operators of affiliate advertising networks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers, ad networks, agencies, and anyone creating or placing native ads must ensure format and disclosures do not mislead. Marketers should ensure partners maintain effective disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: When product-placement or in-context branded appearances do not require disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show that branded billboards in a virtual world or passive product placements that do not convey objective claims may not require disclosure because whether paid or editorial is not material to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the branded appearance conveys claims or would materially affect consumers’ choices; if not material, disclosure may not be necessary. If the placement makes objective claims or implies endorsement, disclose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive/in-app elements that mimic content require disclosure before interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: If an in-app element (icon, item) is formatted like ordinary gameplay/content and tapping it takes the user to advertising, a clear and prominent disclosure informing users of the icon’s commercial nature is necessary before they tap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlay or otherwise label in-game items that are ads so players recognize them as commercial options, especially when they are indistinguishable from gameplay items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-paid search listings and link text should disclose at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: "In non-paid search results, consumers are more likely to notice a disclosure if it’s placed at the beginning of the title tag for a native ad’s search listing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include disclosure at start of the title/snippet or clearly in the URL so users encountering content through search understand its commercial nature before clicking.

rubrics_metrics.name: When republishing or third-party dissemination may create new deception risks
rubrics_metrics.description: An article that is editorial at origin may become advertising when a sponsor pays to promote it via widgets, recommendation services, or placement; the sponsor must ensure claims remain truthful and that the paid nature of the dissemination is disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If distributing or promoting favorable editorial coverage, advertisers must ensure any claims are substantiated and that the paid placement or promotion is disclosed to avoid misleading consumers (see Example 8).
